title: How AI Helps Companies Change the Prices You Pay
summary:
Imagine you and a friend buy the exact same groceries from the same store, but your bill comes out higher. That is the worry behind a new look at how companies use artificial intelligence to set prices.

In one test, 400 shoppers across the United States logged in to Instacart and bought the same 20 items from the same stores, then took screenshots of their carts. The prices were not the same. For some items, the difference was as much as 23 percent. Lindsay Owens, who leads a consumer advocacy group called Groundwork Collaborative, worked with researchers at Consumer Reports and More Perfect Union to study the test.

Soon after it became public, Instacart stopped the experiment. The company said the tests raised concerns and left some people questioning the prices they see on Instacart, adding, "That's not OK." Owens says many companies are comfortable with changing prices, not just for tests. Instead of one price for everyone, companies can now use computer programs called algorithms to shift prices based on personal data.

Owens and her colleague Elizabeth Pancotti also studied 315 patents, which are legal claims over new inventions. They found Walmart patent applications for technology that could connect to a smartwatch and track things like heart rate and blood sugar, and the filings talk about using that information in the ice cream aisle. Walmart plans to put digital price tags in all its U.S. stores by the end of the year, which could let it change prices quickly.

But Walmart executive Dan Bartlett said in an open letter that the company "does not and will not use an individual customer's personal information, income, shopping history, urgency, or willingness to pay to set an individualized price." So will stores charge each shopper a different price? Owens says the technology to do it is already everywhere, powered by data gathering, cloud computing and machine learning. The question now is how companies choose to use it.
why_it_matters: The price you pay for food and other basics could soon depend on data about you, not just the item on the shelf. Knowing how that works helps shoppers ask fair questions before the rules are set.

keywords.explanation: An algorithm is a set of steps a computer program follows to make a choice.
A patent is a legal claim that gives someone the rights to a new invention.
An advocacy group is a group that speaks up for what it thinks is right.
Individualized means made for one single person, not for everyone.
Machine learning is a way for computers to learn from lots of data instead of following fixed rules.
Cloud computing means using powerful computers on the internet instead of one computer at home.

background_read: Stores have always changed prices, for example with sales, but computers now let them change prices for each shopper, using data about what a person buys and how they shop.
Artificial intelligence means computer programs that can spot patterns in huge amounts of data and make choices from them, and companies use it for everything from ads to prices.
A patent is a legal claim over a new invention, and companies file them to protect ideas they may use later, even if the idea never becomes a real product.
Consumer groups study how companies use data and speak up when they think shoppers are being treated unfairly.
